title: Latin America: Maize, Agave & Cane Ferments
attribution: The Americas fermented maize and agave for millennia before contact. Chicha, pulque, tepache and their kin remain living traditions with deep pre-Columbian roots and little statutory definition. Documented from ethnographic and food-science sources; values are typical. (Distilled agave spirits — tequila, mezcal — are covered under their Mexican NOM standards in the Spirits edition.)

styles.name: Chicha de Jora (Maize Beer)
styles.impression: The Andes' ancestral maize beer — cloudy, golden-tan, tart and lightly alcoholic, brewed from sprouted maize and drunk fresh from the chichería.
styles.comments: An Inca state and ritual drink, still central to Andean community life and reciprocal labour (minga). Served in a communal vessel; a red flag or balloon marks a chichería.
styles.ingredients: Jora (malted/germinated maize), boiled and fermented with wild yeast; traditionally some maize was chewed so salivary amylase converted the starch (chicha de muko).

styles.name: Tejuino
styles.impression: A cold, sour-sweet maize drink of western Mexico — fermented masa served over ice with lime, salt and often a scoop of lime sorbet.
styles.comments: Barely alcoholic; sold from street carts in Jalisco and the Pacific coast as a refresher rather than an intoxicant.
styles.ingredients: Masa (nixtamalised maize dough) and piloncillo, cooked, fermented briefly by wild lactic bacteria and yeast.

styles.name: Cauim / Chicha de Yuca
styles.impression: Amazonian and Brazilian indigenous manioc (or maize) beer, traditionally made by chewing the root to saccharify it, then fermenting.
styles.comments: Masato is the Amazonian manioc-chewing version across Peru, Ecuador and Brazil. A communal, ceremonial drink of many Amazonian peoples.
styles.ingredients: Cassava/manioc or maize, cooked and chewed (salivary amylase) or malted, then fermented in a canoe or trough.

styles.name: Pulque (Octli)
styles.impression: The sacred fermented sap of the maguey agave — viscous, milky-white, sour and yeasty-bready, with a slippery texture unlike any other drink.
styles.comments: Predates the Aztecs; hedged with religious ritual and reserved for elders and priests. Nearly killed by beer in the 20th century, now reviving in pulquerías. The viscosity comes from bacterial polysaccharides.
styles.ingredients: Aguamiel (the fresh sap of a mature maguey), fermented by a complex wild culture including Zymomonas mobilis bacteria — one of the few alcohols not primarily yeast-driven.
styles.tags: mexico, pulque, maguey, aguamiel, pre-columbian, traditional

styles.name: Tepache
styles.impression: A lightly fermented pineapple drink of Mexico — sweet-tart, fizzy and refreshing, sold from big glass jars on the street.
styles.comments: Once maize-based (its name is from Nahuatl tepiātl), now overwhelmingly pineapple. Barely alcoholic; a cousin of tepache is the border between soft drink and beer.
styles.ingredients: Pineapple (traditionally the rind), piloncillo and spices, fermented a few days by wild yeast.

styles.name: Guarapo / Cane Wine
styles.impression: Fermented sugarcane juice — sweet, grassy and lightly alcoholic — drunk across the Caribbean and Latin America.
styles.comments: The fermented precursor to cane spirits like cachaça and aguardiente. Also the name for fresh, unfermented cane juice in some regions.
styles.ingredients: Fresh-pressed sugarcane juice fermented by wild yeast.
